title: My solution for learning game dev using an AI Assistant
author: Emergency_Mastodon56
selftext:
Got you. I tightened the tone, removed the AI “voice,” cut the formatting tricks, and kept it closer to how you naturally write. This should read like a real person who actually works in the space, not a content post.

Lately I’ve been noticing a pattern across game dev spaces, especially when new people ask a simple question:

“Where do I start?”

The answers are usually some version of:

learn programming first

start small

watch tutorials

Or sometimes just straight up discouragement.

None of that is completely wrong, but it also doesn’t really help someone take the first step. It just pushes them back without giving them a clear path forward.

So I decided to approach it differently.

For context, I’m finishing a degree in UI/UX, I already have a background in game design, and I work primarily in Unreal using Blueprints. I’m not new to this, but I’m also still actively learning and building.

Instead of focusing on “how should beginners learn,” I started looking at what actually breaks when someone tries to build a game using AI right now.

It’s not capability. AI can generate systems, mechanics, even full design docs.

The problem is structure.

AI doesn’t actually understand your project in a persistent way. Over time, things start to drift. Naming gets inconsistent. Systems stop lining up. You end up spending more time correcting it than building anything new.

It feels less like a tool and more like working with someone who forgets everything between conversations.

That’s the part I’ve been digging into.

I’ve been building out a structured workflow for myself that forces continuity across stages, from design to planning to implementation. The goal isn’t to have AI build the game. The goal is to keep the project coherent so I can actually build it.

The biggest shift for me has been realizing that the hard part isn’t getting AI to generate something. It’s keeping everything connected over time.

Once you solve that, AI stops feeling random and starts feeling useful.

I’m still refining the approach, but it’s already been a much better way to work than just prompting and hoping things line up.

Curious how other people here are handling this.

How are you managing consistency across sessions when using AI for game dev? Are you just re-prompting every time, or have you found a way to keep things grounded?

I am building a web app dev diary and learning tool. It is OS agnostic. Use it on Windows or Mac OS. It is AI agnostic. You choose your AI partner. It is project aware at every step of the way. Check it out, join our discord and join the beta testing in May. I hope to see you there :)
